content: This analysis was conducted by a team of researchers, including Sarah Stansfield, Jesse Heitner, Kate Mitchell, Carla M. Doyle, Rachael M. Milwid, Mathieu Maheu-Giroux, Lise Jamieson, Gesine Meyer-Rath, Leigh Johnson, Jennifer Smith, Andrew Phillips, Marie-Claude Boily, and Dobromir Dimitrov. The study is part of the World Health Organization's (WHO) guidelines and aims to provide insights into the effectiveness, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness of CAB-LA in different populations and geographic regions. CAB-LA has demonstrated superior efficacy compared to daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) for HIV PrEP in the HPTN 083 and 084 trials. It was approved for HIV prevention in the United States in December 2021. The study used four independent HIV transmission models, stratified by age and risk, to evaluate the potential impact of expanding PrEP coverage by introducing CAB-LA. These models were calibrated to local data from Atlanta (HPTN model), Montreal (McGill model), and South Africa (Synthesis and Thembisa models). The analysis simulated scenarios where PrEP coverage was expanded by recruiting additional users based on current PrEP eligibility criteria and switching varying proportions of TDF/FTC users to CAB-LA starting in 2022. In settings with concentrated HIV epidemics, such as among men who have sex with men (MSM) in Atlanta and Montreal, the study found that increasing overall PrEP coverage could significantly reduce new HIV infections. For example, increasing PrEP coverage to 40% of the MSM population in Atlanta by 2027 could avert 35–39% of new HIV infections over 20 years. However, achieving similar reductions in Montreal would require a larger increase in PrEP coverage due to high population-level viral suppression. The cost of averting one disability-adjusted life year (DALY) was estimated to be approximately $200,000 in Atlanta and significantly higher in Montreal. Expanding PrEP coverage to 50% by 2027 could avert nearly 60% of new HIV infections in both cities over 20 years. The analysis suggests that offering CAB-LA to MSM in the USA and Canada could have a substantial impact on the HIV epidemic if it leads to increased overall PrEP coverage. However, while PrEP expansion may be highly efficient and cost-effective in high-incidence settings like Atlanta, it is unlikely to be cost-effective in low-incidence settings like Montreal. In South Africa, where the HIV epidemic is generalized, current PrEP coverage is below 1% and is not expected to increase significantly by 2042 under base-case scenarios. Expanding PrEP coverage to 13% of the adult population by 2027, primarily targeting high-risk groups with CAB-LA, could avert approximately 20% of new HIV infections over 20 years. Targeted use of CAB-LA during periods of substantial HIV risk could avert nearly 50% of new infections over the same period. In comparison, similar expansion using oral TDF/FTC instead of CAB-LA would result in a 20–40% reduction in impact due to lower efficacy and adherence. The analysis estimates that 16–25 additional person-years (PYs) on CAB-LA are needed to prevent one infection in South Africa with strict risk targeting, compared to over 100 PYs if CAB-LA is broadly available but primarily used by high-risk individuals. The findings suggest that offering CAB-LA in South Africa could significantly impact the HIV epidemic if it is adequately used by individuals at high risk of acquiring HIV. PrEP expansion could be highly efficient and cost-effective if adopted primarily during periods of substantial risk. However, the cost-effectiveness of CAB-LA depends on the setting, population, and implementation strategy.
